title: Shelbyville
summary: Shelbyville rose on land William Shannon gave as the seat of Shelby County, carved from Jefferson County in 1792 and named for first governor Isaac Shelby.
bodyMarkdown:
Shelbyville was created in 1792, the year Kentucky became a state. Its founding gave a new county a seat along the road between Frankfort and the Falls of the Ohio. Settlers had already been in the area for more than a decade.

## Before the town

The first permanent settlement in what is now Shelby County was [Squire Boone's Painted Stone Station](/stories/squire-boones-painted-stone/). Daniel Boone's brother Squire [explored](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelbyville,_Kentucky) the area as early as 1775 and built the station in spring 1780 on the Clear Fork of Brashear's Creek. Elsewhere the same entry dates it to "around 1779–1780."

## A county and a gift of land

Shelby County was formed from Jefferson County on June 28, 1792. It was named for [Isaac Shelby](/stories/isaac-shelby-old-kings-mountain/), Kentucky's first governor.

At the first meeting of the county court that October, landowner William Shannon agreed to give 50 acres for a town and 1 more acre for public buildings. An account of [Shelbyville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelbyville,_Kentucky) says the grant is why Shelbyville, rather than nearby Squire Boone's Station, became the county seat.

## A log-cabin town

The town stood on the west bank of Clear Creek where Mulberry Creek joins it. New residents had to build a 1½-story log cabin with a stone chimney. By 1795 there were 40 such cabins, and by 1800 the town had 262 residents.

The town was formally incorporated in 1846. Shelby County later [led](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelbyville,_Kentucky) Kentucky in hog production by 1870.

## Civil War violence

Shelby County saw guerrilla fighting during the Civil War. The [January 25, 1865, attack](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelbyville,_Kentucky) near Simpsonville on Black soldiers of the 5th U.S. Colored Cavalry. They were driving about 900 cattle from [Camp Nelson](/stories/camp-nelson-kentucky-us-colored-troops/) toward Louisville when guerrillas struck. Accounts of the killings differ: [one account](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelbyville,_Kentucky) says about 22 soldiers died near Simpsonville, while [another, on Shelby County](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shelby_County,_Kentucky), counts 35 Union cattle drivers killed in the county. Where they were buried remains under investigation.

In response to the killing of Union cattle drivers and to William Quantrill's arrival in Kentucky, Union authorities paid a Shelby County Home Guard unit under Edwin Terrell. On May 10, 1865, Terrell's men caught Quantrill's band in Spencer County and fatally shot Quantrill.

## Kentucky today

Shelbyville remains the Shelby County seat and had 17,282 residents at the 2020 census. Interstate 64 links it to Louisville and Lexington. Its historic Main Street draws shoppers and visitors, and parks along Clear Creek offer trails and recreation.
